original_question: Is every element in Diff ∞ + (S ) a commutator?
target_in_paper: Section 7.1, Question 7.1 (Frédéric Le Roux): the paper asks exactly whether every element of Diff^\infty_+(S^1) is a commutator. ([conferences.cirm-math.fr](https://conferences.cirm-math.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Problem_list_3082.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the intended yes/no problem, the universal quantifier ('every element'), the ambient group up to slightly incomplete notation, and the fact that the issue is being a single commutator rather than merely a product of commutators. This matches Question 7.1, not the neighboring surface question in Question 7.2. ([conferences.cirm-math.fr](https://conferences.cirm-math.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Problem_list_3082.pdf))
missing_details: Replace the incomplete manifold notation 'S' by the circle S^1. ([conferences.cirm-math.fr](https://conferences.cirm-math.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Problem_list_3082.pdf))

Spell out that Diff^\infty_+(S^1) means the group of orientation-preserving C^\infty diffeomorphisms of the circle; the '+' and the smoothness class are part of the paper's statement. ([conferences.cirm-math.fr](https://conferences.cirm-math.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Problem_list_3082.pdf))

Make explicit that 'a commutator' means a single commutator [g,h] = ghg^{-1}h^{-1} with g,h \in Diff^\infty_+(S^1). The subsection introduces commutators and commutator length immediately before the question. ([conferences.cirm-math.fr](https://conferences.cirm-math.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Problem_list_3082.pdf))

For a stand-alone formulation, it helps to state the quantified element as f \in Diff^\infty_+(S^1). ([conferences.cirm-math.fr](https://conferences.cirm-math.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Problem_list_3082.pdf))

No extra hypothesis such as a Diophantine rotation number belongs in the question itself; that condition appears only in the motivating discussion explaining why every element is known to be a product of two commutators. ([conferences.cirm-math.fr](https://conferences.cirm-math.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Problem_list_3082.pdf))
refined_question: Is every orientation-preserving C^\infty diffeomorphism of the circle a single commutator in Diff^\infty_+(S^1)? Equivalently: for every f \in Diff^\infty_+(S^1), do there exist g,h \in Diff^\infty_+(S^1) such that f = [g,h] = ghg^{-1}h^{-1}? ([conferences.cirm-math.fr](https://conferences.cirm-math.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Problem_list_3082.pdf))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, is the commutator length on Diff^\infty_+(S^1) at most 1 for every element? This uses the subsection's definition of commutator length as word length with respect to the set of commutators. ([conferences.cirm-math.fr](https://conferences.cirm-math.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Problem_list_3082.pdf))
justification: The nearby context in Section 7.1 first defines word length, stable word length, commutator length, and stable commutator length. It then states that, by Herman's theorem and continuity of the rotation number, every element of Diff^\infty_+(S^1) is already known to be a product of two commutators, and identifies the remaining sharp open issue as whether one commutator always suffices. That is exactly what your draft is aiming at, so the paper-faithful refinement is simply to make the notation and the meaning of 'commutator' fully explicit, without broadening to other manifolds or regularity classes. ([conferences.cirm-math.fr](https://conferences.cirm-math.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Problem_list_3082.pdf))
